options.explanation: Aluminium is not a magnetic substance.
Steel is magnetic — it can be induced.
Iron is the classic magnetic element.
Nickel is one of the magnetic elements.

options.text: a magnet made in a factory
options.explanation: Manufacture is irrelevant; the field-driven mechanism defines induction.

options.text: a magnetic material magnetised while in another magnet's field
options.explanation: Induction is field-driven, temporary magnetisation.

options.text: a magnet that keeps its field for years
options.explanation: That describes a permanent magnet.

options.text: a non-magnetic material pulled by a magnet
options.explanation: Non-magnetic materials are never pulled.

questions.stem: The force between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet is always:

options.explanation: Induction exists precisely to produce the pull.
The force weakens with distance but stays attractive.
Induction puts an unlike pole nearest, so the pair attracts.
Repulsion needs two independent magnets with like poles facing.

questions.stem: A paperclip sticks to a magnet. The magnet is removed and the clip no longer holds a second clip. What type of magnetic material is the clip?

options.explanation: A hard material would keep the induced magnetism.
It was attracted, so it is a magnetic substance.
A permanent clip would keep holding the second one.
Losing magnetism as soon as the field goes is soft behaviour.

questions.stem: Which set lists ONLY permanent-magnet behaviour?

options.text: keeps its field with no external help; can repel another magnet
options.explanation: Sustained field plus pole interaction are permanent traits.

options.text: gains poles only near a magnet; loses them when removed
options.explanation: That is induced behaviour.

options.text: attracted to either pole; never repels
options.explanation: Attraction-only describes induced magnets or raw magnetic materials.
Hard permanent magnets resist casual demagnetising.

questions.stem: Name four magnetic elements or their alloys.
questions.modelAnswer: Iron, steel, cobalt and nickel — steel being the iron alloy used for permanent magnets.

questions.stem: State what is always true about the force between a magnet and an unmagnetised magnetic material.
questions.modelAnswer: The force is always attraction, whatever pole of the magnet is presented.

questions.stem: Explain why an induced magnet always attracts the magnet that induces it.
questions.modelAnswer: The field aligns the material's domains so an induced pole forms at its near face that is unlike the facing pole of the magnet. Unlike poles attract, so the interaction is a pull no matter which pole was presented — the geometry of induction guarantees attraction.

questions.stem: A technician sorts scrap with a magnet: some pieces stick and stay stuck after release; others fall straight off. Sort the pieces by magnetic class and name each class.
questions.modelAnswer: Pieces that stay magnetised after release are made of magnetically hard material and behave as permanent magnets. Pieces that fall straight off were induced magnets of soft magnetic material — they held poles only while in the field.

questions.stem: Which material suits a PERMANENT magnet?

options.explanation: Plastics carry no magnetic response.
Hard materials retain their aligned domains permanently.
Soft iron sheds its magnetism when the field leaves.
Copper is non-magnetic.

questions.stem: A north pole is held near one end of an iron bar. What pole appears at that near end?

options.explanation: The field induces poles in the bar.

options.text: both poles at the same end
options.explanation: One face carries one induced pole.
Induction always puts the unlike pole nearest.
A near north pole would repel — induction instead attracts.

questions.stem: When the magnet is taken away from the iron bar, the bar:

options.text: keeps its full induced magnetism forever
options.explanation: Permanent retention is hard-material behaviour; the bar is soft iron.
Nothing reverses; the induced poles simply fade.
It can be induced again at any time.

options.text: loses most of its induced magnetism
options.explanation: Induced magnetism persists only while the field is present.

questions.stem: Which observation shows a bar is a PERMANENT magnet rather than an induced one?

options.text: it still attracts pins an hour after being far from any other magnet
options.explanation: Field-free retention is the permanent signature.
Both permanent and induced magnets attract.
Material alone does not settle the magnetisation state.

options.text: it hangs pointing north-south when freely suspended
options.explanation: Earth's field induces that alignment even in soft materials.

questions.stem: Steel is described as magnetically HARD. What does 'hard' mean here?

options.explanation: Heating is not part of the hard/soft definition.

options.text: it keeps its magnetism and resists demagnetising
options.explanation: Hardness refers to retention, not physical scratch resistance.

options.text: it is difficult to cut or drill
options.explanation: Mechanical hardness is not the magnetic meaning.

options.text: it feels hard to the touch
options.explanation: Texture is irrelevant to the magnetic class.

questions.stem: State what a permanent magnet does that an induced magnet cannot.
questions.modelAnswer: A permanent magnet keeps its magnetic field without any external field present.

questions.stem: State the pole that appears on the near face of an iron bar next to a south pole.
questions.modelAnswer: A north pole is induced on the near face, unlike the facing south pole.

questions.stem: Explain why the paperclip chain collapses the instant the top magnet is lifted away.
questions.modelAnswer: Every clip in the chain held only induced magnetism, created by the field of the magnet and of the clips above it. Lifting the magnet removes the top field, so the first clip loses its poles and drops; losing it removes the field for the second, and the collapse cascades down the chain.

questions.stem: A magnetic door catch must hold the door firmly whenever it is near the frame plate but must never interfere when the door is open. Design the catch's magnetic pairing and justify it.
questions.modelAnswer: Fix a small permanent magnet in the frame and fit a soft iron plate on the door. Whenever the door nears the frame the plate becomes an induced magnet and is attracted firmly to the permanent magnet, latching the door; with the door open the plate holds no magnetism, so it does nothing until it is close again.
